web_evidence.title: Excerpt from The Nickel Boys
web_evidence.note: The publisher's authorized opening excerpt narrates the Nickel investigation and adult Elwood externally in sustained third-person prose.

web_evidence.title: African American Affective Space, Memory, and Cultural Trauma in Colson Whitehead's The Nickel Boys
web_evidence.note: The scholarly article explicitly identifies multiple limited-omniscient third-person narrations centered successively on teenage Elwood, Turner, and adult Elwood/Turner.

web_evidence.title: Interview: Filmmaker RaMell Ross on Choosing Perspective for Nickel Boys, Casting Fresh Faces and the Timing of Historical Narratives
web_evidence.note: In discussing why the film required an invented first-person visual language, adapter RaMell Ross explicitly states that the book is entirely third person.

web_evidence.title: The Nickel Boys Literary Elements
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly describes a third-person narrator closely following Elwood and Turner and explains the apparent adult-Elwood perspective revealed to be Turner.

person_note: The Goodreads passages repeatedly show a nonparticipating narrator naming Elwood, Turner, Harriet, and others while entering their thoughts through third-person limited and free-indirect narration. First-person plural language belongs to embedded Martin Luther King Jr. speeches, direct dialogue, or authorial acknowledgments, while apparent you narration is generic, conversational, or focalized free-indirect language rather than a sustained second-person strand. The authorized opening corroborates third-person prose, and whole-book scholarly analysis explicitly establishes multiple third-person focal centers; multiple focal characters and timelines do not constitute a change in grammatical person. No credible evidence of a sustained first- or second-person base section was found.
